text: The first weekend of that month I took the long route up the ridge alone, something I had wanted to do for years and kept postponing. The morning was clear. By the time I reached the shoulder of the hill it was not, and the cloud came down so completely that the cairns disappeared one by one until I was standing on a slope of wet rock with no idea which direction was down. I waited. I ate the second sandwich. I counted to a hundred several times for no reason I can defend. After an hour or so the cloud thinned enough to show a line of fence posts, and I followed them to a track and the track to the car, and I sat in the driver's seat for a long time before I turned the key. I do not know how to file that day as either good or bad. The hour on the rock was the loneliest I had spent in a decade, and the view when it finally opened was the finest I have ever seen, and I would not trade one for the other. What that day taught me is that waiting is a skill and not a failure, and that a place can frighten you and still be worth going back to. I went back in the autumn. The cairns were all there, exactly where they had been the whole time.

I don't want to write this and I'm going to anyway.

Driving my nephew back from his swimming lesson this afternoon, a van came through the junction and hit the back passenger side. The side he was sitting on. The car spun half round and stopped against the kerb. For a few seconds nothing made any sense, and then I heard him crying, which was the best sound in the world because it meant he was awake and breathing.

He is fine. They checked him over for three hours and he is fine, bruised along the arm where the belt held him, and already telling everyone at home about the fire engine. I am fine, apparently.

I keep going over it, and the thing I keep arriving at is this: I was the one in the driver's seat. I was the adult he was handed over to, the one who was supposed to get him home. That is where I was in all of this, and that is where I will be in it whenever my sister looks at me for the next while.

And the other thing, which I need to say plainly: the van driver did this. He came through without stopping, the witness said so, the marks on the road say so. It was not me. I was doing nothing wrong. He did this.

I still hate that it happened on my watch. I hate that it was my car and my afternoon and my nephew in the back.

No more tonight.

Small, odd day. Nothing to report except the kettle. It stopped working mid-boil this morning and I spent forty minutes taking the base apart with a butter knife before admitting it was dead and walking to the shop for a new one. My partner found this funny. I found it a bit funny and a bit annoying, in roughly equal halves.

A few notes since I'm here anyway. My shoulders were tight the whole time I was crouched over it, which I only noticed because I kept rolling them. It was my fault it broke, probably, I've been overfilling it for months and the manual says not to. And I'm aware that I'm the one in this house who has to try to fix things before I'll let anyone buy a replacement; that's just the seat I sit in. I've always been like that about frustration, I keep a lid on it and go quiet and fiddle with screws rather than say out loud that I'm annoyed. Partner knows this, makes tea in a saucepan, and waits.

What I learned, if a kettle can teach anything, is that forty minutes is my limit before I'll admit defeat. I'm writing it down so I can check that number next time something breaks, that's all this entry is for.

New kettle is blue. It's fine. Day was fine.

User: The results came out. I didn't pass.
Assistant: I'm sorry. That's a hard thing to read after a year of work. Do you want to talk about it, or just sit with it for a minute?
User: I don't know. I've read the email four times. I was two marks short. Two.
Assistant: Two marks is close enough to feel cruel. How are you doing right now, physically?
User: My hands have been shaking since I opened it. I had to put the mug down. And there's a cold feeling in my stomach that won't go.
Assistant: That makes sense. Shock sits in the body before it sits anywhere else. You don't have to do anything with it yet.
User: Everyone at work knows I sat it. My manager asked me about it this morning and I just said "still waiting". I lied to his face.
Assistant: You bought yourself a day. That's not a crime. What's the part that stings most?
User: I'm the one who passes things. That's who I've been since school. I was the kid who passed, I'm the colleague who passes. I don't know how to be in the room as the person who didn't.
Assistant: That's a real loss, and it's a different loss from the marks themselves. It's about where you stand with people.
User: Yeah. I can't even think about the resit yet. I just want to not have to say it out loud to anyone.
Assistant: Then don't, tonight. Tonight can be about getting through the evening. The telling can wait until you've chosen the words.
User: OK. I'm going to turn this off and lie down.
Assistant: That sounds right. I'm here whenever you want to pick it up again.

Quick one. I finally got the sourdough to rise properly. Fourth attempt, and this time it actually came out of the oven looking like the pictures, with the ear and the open crumb and the whole business. Ate half of it with butter, standing at the counter, still warm.

What it taught me is that the slow way is the right way with this; leave it alone overnight and it does the work by itself. I'd been poking at it every hour on the earlier attempts like it owed me something.

It has also, honestly, changed my whole weekend. Nothing is the same about Saturday mornings now; there's a thing to check on, a thing to shape, a reason to be up and about before nine with the radio on. I like it more than I expected to.

I'm noting the overnight trick here so I remember to do it next time rather than reading six forum threads again. That's the only point of this entry.

Loaf: good. Toast tomorrow: better. Mood: good.

My sister came round tonight. She didn't text first, she just turned up with a bag of oranges and the nephew's drawing of the fire engine, and stood in the hall until I let her in.

We talked for four hours. Four. I don't think we've done that since we were teenagers sharing a room. She said she had been angry for about a day and then had sat with it and was not angry anymore, and that she had needed to come and say that to my face rather than over the phone. Then she asked how I was, and waited, and actually listened to the answer.

Somewhere around the second hour I noticed my shoulders had come down from around my ears and my chest had gone loose and warm, the way it does after a hot bath. I hadn't realised how tightly I'd been holding everything for nine days.

I want to be fair about this: the credit is hers. She made the first move, she walked over here, she chose the oranges and the drawing. I was still hiding behind one-line texts. Whatever happened tonight happened because she decided it would.

What it means, I think, is that the two of us are still a family that repairs things, even now, even when it's hard.

She left at midnight and hugged me in the doorway for a long time. The nephew's drawing is on the fridge, slightly crooked, held up with the magnet shaped like a lemon.

User: Finished the shelf. It's up. It's also about a centimetre off level.
Assistant: Congratulations on getting it up. How do you feel about the centimetre?
User: Half proud, half irritated. It holds books, which was the brief. But I can see the tilt from the sofa and now I can't un-see it.
Assistant: Both of those can be true at once. Do you know where the tilt came from?
User: Yes, that part's on me. I measured from the floor once instead of using the level, because I was in a hurry to get it done before dinner. Nobody else to blame, it was my shortcut.
Assistant: That's a very honest post-mortem for a shelf.
User: Ha. I want to log this with you so that next time I'm about to skip a step on a build, you can remind me about the sofa view. That's what I want this one kept for.
Assistant: Noted. I'll bring it up when the next project comes around.
User: Thanks. It does look good with the books on, to be fair. The plants hide the worst of it.
Assistant: Then it's a working shelf with a story. How are the brackets?
User: I used the brass ones, the good ones, so at least it's a well-dressed tilt.
Assistant: A tilt with standards. Enjoy the books.

Session 6. Client arrived on time, presentation flat but engaged. Session focused on a minor interpersonal event from the past week: a friend cancelled a planned coffee for the second time this month by text, approximately an hour beforehand.

Client described irritation and a low mood that lasted the rest of the evening, which they rated as mild and noted had passed by the following morning. Client was clear that the event itself was "small" and "not the point".

Client attributed the cancellation to the friend's chronic disorganisation rather than to any change in the friendship, stating, "She's like this with everyone, it isn't about me." Clinician noted that this differs from the self-blaming attributions reported in earlier sessions.

Client described their position in this friendship, and in most friendships, as "the one who does the chasing, the one who books the table and sends the reminder". Client expressed some fatigue with this role but no wish to change it at present.

Client offered the following self-description: "I get clingy when people go quiet. I always have. Even a two-hour delay in replying and I'm checking my phone every few minutes." Clinician noted the pattern as consistent with themes raised at intake.

When asked what the episode meant to them, client stated, "What it tells me is that I can be annoyed at a friend without it turning into a crisis about whether they still like me." Clinician affirmed this.

Plan: continue monitoring attribution style in low-stakes interpersonal events. Homework: notice one instance of waiting for a reply without checking. Next session as scheduled.

User: Quiz night. We came ninth out of eleven.
Assistant: Ouch. Was that lower than usual for your team?
User: We're normally top four. I got the whole geography round wrong. The whole round. Five questions.
Assistant: That's a rough round. How are you feeling about it now you're home?
User: Grumpy. It's not a big thing, I know it's not, but I'm the one on that team who's meant to know the capitals and the rivers. That's my corner. Everyone else does sport or music or films. I do maps. And tonight I didn't.
Assistant: So it's less about ninth place and more about the corner you hold.
User: Yeah. Exactly that. If I'm not the maps person, what am I bringing? A pen?
Assistant: You're bringing you, which your team presumably likes. But I hear that the maps thing matters.
User: What I'm taking from it, honestly, is that I care about this more than I'd admit. A pub quiz, and I care. That's the lesson, if there is one.
Assistant: That's a fair read, and not a bad thing to find out.
User: Maybe. Right now I just want to be grumpy for an hour and then forget it.
Assistant: An hour of grumpiness is a reasonable budget for ninth place. Enjoy it.

Session 7. Client presented brighter than in recent weeks, with more spontaneous speech. Session opened with client reporting a small success from the working week: they had volunteered to give the five-minute update at a team meeting, something they had declined to do on several previous occasions.

Client reported that the update went "fine, unremarkable, which is the point". Client described noticing, during the update, that their voice stayed steady, and that afterwards "my shoulders dropped about two inches and I could feel my breathing go slow again, like after a run". Clinician reflected this as useful body awareness.

Client described their usual position in the team as "the quiet one at the end of the table, the one who takes the notes and emails them round afterwards". Client noted with some humour that someone else had to take the notes this week.

Clinician asked what, if anything, client took from the experience. Client stated: "What it shows me is that I can do the small public things and nothing bad happens. Not that I'll love them, just that they're survivable." Clinician affirmed this as a realistic appraisal.

Client was careful to frame the event as minor and did not want to "make a thing of it". Clinician agreed that it need not be more than it was, while noting that it is relevant to the goals set at intake.

Mood: mildly positive, stable. Risk: none identified. Plan: continue graded practice with low-stakes speaking tasks. Next session as scheduled.

User: Day one hundred. And I did the wedding last night without a single drink.
Assistant: One hundred days, and a wedding on top. That's enormous. How was it?
User: Honestly, good. Better than good. I was the one at the table with the sparkling water and the lime, and for the first time I was fine being that one. I didn't apologise for it. I didn't explain. Somebody asked and I said "not tonight" and that was the end of it.
Assistant: That sounds like a very different room from the ones you've described before.
User: It was. And this morning. Clear head, no pounding behind the eyes, hands completely steady while I made coffee. I stood there just noticing my hands.
Assistant: Noticing steady hands is a milestone most people never get to have.
User: I want to say something and I want you to keep it. I did this. Not the app, not the meetings, not my partner nagging. Me, sitting through every single evening when the easy thing was right there. I get to own this one.
Assistant: You do. Kept.
User: And keep the reason. I'm telling you so there's a record I can read back on the next bad night, when my brain is telling me one won't matter. That's what this is for.
Assistant: That's a good use of a record. I'll surface it whenever you ask.
User: Because here's the thing about me, and I know this: I've always reached for something to take the edge off. I don't sit with feelings, I numb them. That's been my pattern since I was a teenager.
Assistant: And last night you sat with a whole wedding's worth of feelings.
User: I did. And something flipped. Last night was the moment it turned. Nothing about how I see myself is the same as it was on Friday afternoon.
Assistant: Then today is worth marking. Congratulations on one hundred, and on the room.

User: Nearly got flattened by a delivery bike this morning. Stepped off the kerb by the bakery and it was just there, inches away.
Assistant: That sounds frightening. Are you hurt at all?
User: No, it missed me. Didn't even touch me. I'm fine, just rattled, and a bit cross.
Assistant: Rattled makes sense. What did it feel like in the moment?
User: My heart went like a drum for about a minute afterwards and my legs felt wobbly walking to the office. It settled by the time I got to my desk.
Assistant: That's the body doing its job. Did anything you did make a difference?
User: No, and that's the annoying part. It was pure luck. I didn't see it, I didn't jump, it just happened to swerve. Nothing I did saved me. Chance, start to finish.
Assistant: That's an uncomfortable thing to sit with. Do you want to take anything from it?
User: Only this: what it's taught me is that that corner is blind from the bakery side and I should cross further up. Small lesson, cheap price.
Assistant: Cheap compared to the alternative.
User: I'm telling you mainly so I remember it. If I ever mention the bakery again, I want it to prompt me to cross at the lights. That's all it's for.
Assistant: Logged. Bakery means cross at the lights.
User: Right. Anyway. A nothing sort of day otherwise. Back to the spreadsheet.

There was a Sunday that month we drove out to the coast, the two of us, because the week had been dull and we wanted a horizon. It was, in short, a disappointing day, and not one I would otherwise have remembered. The sea was the colour of dishwater and the café we liked had changed hands and now served everything in paper, and the walk along the front was shorter and shabbier than either of us recalled. We sat in the car for a while with the heater on and watched a dog refuse to go into the water. On the drive home we were quiet, not bickering, just flat, the way you are when an outing has not paid out and nobody wants to be the first to say so. It would have been forgotten entirely except for a small thought I had on the motorway, which has outlasted the day itself: what I took from that Sunday is that the places I loved at twenty-five are not obliged to stay the same for me, and that going back to check is a kind of tax I will keep paying anyway. The dog never did go in. We did not stop for chips. We were home before dark, which felt like the final insult.

They packed a bag tonight. Not everything, a bag. Said they needed a few weeks at their brother's to think, and that it wasn't a decision, it was a pause, and that they would call on the weekend. Then the door, and the car, and the sound of the car getting smaller.

I'm not going to try to make sense of it tonight. I'm not going to go back through the last six months looking for the place it started. I know I will do that eventually and I know I'll do it badly, and I want to not do it yet.

What I will do is put down exactly what was said, because in a week this will have softened or hardened in my head, and I want the true version to exist somewhere. That's what this entry is for. Not to process. To keep.

They said: "I love you and I don't know if I'm happy." They said: "This isn't a leaving." They said: "Please don't text tonight." They took the grey jumper and the book from the bedside and the good pillow. They left their keys on the hook, which could mean they're coming back or could mean nothing at all.

The flat is very large. The fridge is making the noise it makes. I've left the hall light on, which is stupid, and I'm not going to turn it off.

I haven't texted.

PASSED.

Writing it in capitals because I shouted it in capitals. Opened the email on the stairs and read the number three times and then made a noise I don't think I've ever made and sat down right there on the step, because my knees actually went, a proper wobble, and my face was hot for about ten minutes after.

Twelve marks over. Not scraping. Twelve.

I rang my sister first. She screamed. The nephew screamed because she was screaming. Then I rang my manager, who said "I knew it", which he did not, but it was nice of him.

Here's what I want to say while it's fresh. I earned this one. Not luck, not an easy paper. Me, at the kitchen table, every evening for five weeks with the lamp on and the phone in the other room. Nobody else did those evenings. I did.

And I'm not the one who passes anymore. That version got broken in the winter and I'm glad, because the one I am now is the one who failed and came back. That's a better seat to sit in. I like it better here.

This is the line, I think. There's before this email and there's after it, and I can already feel that I'm going to count things from today.

Going out for dinner with my sister. Sparkling water, and I don't even mind.

User: Small fire in the kitchen. Put out. Everything's fine. Flat smells awful.
Assistant: I'm glad you're okay. What happened?
User: Tea towel. I'd left it draped over the edge of the hob and the ring was still warm, more than warm apparently. Came back from the loo to a flame about the size of my hand. Smothered it with the lid of the big pan.
Assistant: Quick thinking with the lid. How are you feeling now?
User: Annoyed and a bit shaky. My hands were trembling for a good ten minutes after, I had to sit on the kitchen step and wait for them to stop before I could open the window.
Assistant: That's a normal reaction to a fright. It wasn't nothing.
User: It wasn't anyone else's fault, let's be clear. My towel, my hob, my not checking. Entirely my own doing.
Assistant: Owning it is fair, as long as you're not being cruel to yourself about it.
User: I'm more embarrassed than cruel. I'm supposed to be the careful one in this flat. I'm the one who checks the door twice and turns the plugs off at the wall. That's my job here. And I'm the one who set fire to the kitchen.
Assistant: Even the careful one gets a tea towel wrong occasionally.
User: Put it on the list, though. If I mention cooking late at night, remind me about the towel. I want this one kept so it does some good.
Assistant: Done. I'll remind you.
User: Right. Opening every window in the place. Talk later.

Session 10. Client on time, mood described as "okay, actually". Client chose to begin with a positive interpersonal event rather than the ongoing material from previous sessions, and clinician followed the client's lead.

Client reported that a neighbour from the floor below, with whom they had previously exchanged only greetings, knocked on the door midweek to return a misdelivered parcel and stayed for a cup of tea. The conversation lasted approximately forty minutes and covered the building, the neighbour's allotment, and a shared dislike of the new recycling bins. Client described the exchange as "nice, easy, nothing in it", and smiled while recounting it.

Clinician asked what, if anything, the client made of the encounter. Client stated: "I suppose it means that company doesn't have to be a big arrangement. Someone can just knock, and that counts." Clinician reflected this back and client agreed with the summary.

Client did not elaborate further and did not link the event to any wider pattern. Clinician did not press, in keeping with the agreed pacing. Remainder of session was spent on the sleep diary, which shows modest improvement in time to sleep onset, and on scheduling around the client's work commitments.

Mood at close: mildly positive. Risk: none identified. Plan: continue sleep diary; next session as scheduled.

User: Spent an hour and forty minutes on hold with the energy supplier this afternoon. Then got cut off.
Assistant: An hour and forty minutes, and then nothing. That's a bad afternoon.
User: Yeah. It's not important. Nothing happened. That's sort of the problem, nothing happened and the whole afternoon's gone.
Assistant: Did you get it sorted in the end?
User: No. I'll have to try again. I'm just flat about it. The hold music was the same four bars. I could hum it for you.
Assistant: Please don't. Is there anything you want to do with this, or just vent?
User: Mostly vent. Although, I'll say this. What it tells me is that I'll sit through almost anything rather than hang up and lose my place. An hour and forty minutes. That's a bit of a lesson about me.
Assistant: It's a kind of persistence that sometimes pays off.
User: Not today. Anyway, keep this one. Next time I say I'm going to ring them, remind me to use the web chat or do it first thing in the morning. That's all I want this for, so I don't do another afternoon like this.
Assistant: Kept. Ring early or use the chat.
User: Thanks. Going to make dinner and pretend the afternoon was a dream.
Assistant: A forgettable one, hopefully. Enjoy dinner.

Ran into someone from the old flat today, in the queue at the pharmacy of all places. I hadn't seen her in five years. The last time we spoke I was supposed to be at her father's funeral and I was not, and I never explained, and I never answered the three messages she sent afterwards.

She said my name first. I almost pretended not to hear.

We ended up in the café next door for an hour. I told her the truth about that year, all of it, the parts I'd never said out loud to anyone. She listened. She didn't let me off. She said it had hurt, a lot, and that she had spent a long time wondering why. Then she said she was glad I'd said it now, and asked how long I'd been sober, and I told her, and she said "good" and squeezed my hand across the table.

I don't know what we are now. We swapped numbers. We said the thing people say about coffee.

Walking home I felt two things at once and I'm still feeling both. The first is relief, plain relief, like putting down a bag I'd carried so long I'd stopped noticing the weight. The second is the plain old shame, not smaller, just finally out in the open where she could see it too.

I'm glad it was the pharmacy. I'm glad there was a queue. I'm glad she said my name before I could decide whether to say hers.

Grey day. Nothing in it.

The train was late, then it was crowded, then it stopped outside the station for twenty minutes with nobody saying why. Work was the same spreadsheet as yesterday and will be the same spreadsheet tomorrow. Lunch was a sandwich eaten at the desk. Somebody's birthday cake in the kitchen, the kind with the thick icing; I had a slice and didn't want it.

There was a dull ache behind my eyes from about two o'clock onward, the kind that doesn't become anything but doesn't go either, and my neck was stiff from the train, and by the time I got home I had the tired-but-not-sleepy thing where you lie on the sofa and can't be bothered to reach for the remote.

Ate toast for dinner. Talked to nobody. Looked at the hall light for a while.

A nothing day, and a low one. I'll have forgotten it by the weekend, which is fine.

Bed.

Session 12. Client arrived slightly late, apologised, settled quickly. Affect notably more animated than in recent sessions, with some tearfulness toward the end.

Session was given almost entirely to the client's account of a three-day walking trip taken alone over the long weekend, which client had booked some weeks ago and had considered cancelling. Client described the trip as "the biggest thing that's happened to me in months, and I'm not sure if it was good".

Client described the first evening in the hostel as very difficult: "my stomach was knotted up the whole evening, I couldn't eat the dinner I'd paid for, and I lay there with my jaw clenched listening to other people laughing downstairs". On the second day, on the hill, client reported the knot loosening by mid-morning and "not coming back". Client described the summit as "quiet, enormous, and I cried for about ten minutes and didn't mind".

Client was asked what the trip meant to them. Client stated: "What it taught me is that I can be on my own and be all right. Not happy, necessarily. All right." Client became tearful here and clinician allowed silence.

Client stated unprompted that they want to hold on to this memory for a specific reason: "I want to keep it so that next time I'm dreading an empty weekend I can point at it and say, you did three days, you were fine. It's evidence. That's what it's for." Clinician affirmed the use of concrete experience as counter-evidence.

Client declined to discuss partner contact this session. Mood: mixed, with pride and grief both present and both named by client. Plan: revisit next session; continue sleep diary.

User: Bit of a sour one with my sister this evening. Nothing dramatic.
Assistant: What happened?
User: I was twenty minutes late picking up the nephew from football and she'd had to hang around in the car park with him. She was short with me. Didn't shout, just that voice. Then "see you Thursday" and drove off.
Assistant: That voice can land harder than shouting. How are you with it?
User: Not great. A bit sore. I don't like it when she's clipped with me, and I know I'll be chewing on it at bedtime.
Assistant: Was there anything behind the lateness?
User: No excuse, really. It was my doing. I knew the time and I let a work call run on because I didn't want to cut the client off. That's the whole of it. Her being annoyed is fair.
Assistant: That's a clear-eyed account. Do you want to do anything with it?
User: Yes, actually. Keep this one. I want it on file so the next time I've got the nephew pickup you can nudge me half an hour before, and so I remember how that car park conversation felt. That's what I want it for.
Assistant: Kept. A nudge half an hour before pickups, and the car park.
User: Thanks. Going to text her goodnight and leave it there.
Assistant: That sounds like the right size of response. Goodnight.

Session 13. Client arrived early and began speaking before sitting down. Affect labile across the session, moving between flat and animated. Client stated at the outset that they had "news" and wished to use the whole session on it.

Client reported that their partner returned to the flat at the weekend, by arrangement, for a conversation about the pause begun several weeks ago. Client described the conversation as lasting most of an afternoon and ending with an agreement to separate. Client reported that the partner will collect the remainder of their belongings over the coming fortnight and that both parties have agreed to a period of no contact afterwards.

Client was notably clear about their own role in the conversation. Client stated: "I'm the one who said it. Not them. I was the one who put it on the table and said we should stop, and I want to be clear about that." Client returned to this framing several times and appeared to draw some steadiness from it.

Client described the week since as "grief and relief taking turns, sometimes within the same hour". Client reported sleeping better than expected and also being unexpectedly upset in the supermarket. Client did not seek to resolve the two feelings into one and clinician did not encourage this.

Client stated: "This is the hinge. Whatever my life looks like from here, it is not going to look like the one I had before Sunday. Everything is going to date from that afternoon." Clinician reflected the weight of this and client agreed.

Client did not offer an account of why the relationship ended and clinician did not pursue this today. Plan: hold space for the separation process; review support network next session; continue sleep diary.

User: Second shelf is up. Level. Dead level. I checked it three times.
Assistant: Redemption for the sofa view. How does it feel?
User: Good. Small good. My arms ache in that nice way from holding the drill up for an hour, and I've got that warm tired feeling across my shoulders like after swimming.
Assistant: Earned aches. What made the difference this time?
User: Me, honestly. I used the level at every stage and I didn't rush it for dinner. You reminded me, like I asked, but I'm claiming this one: I did the slow version and the slow version worked. Credit where it's due and it's due to me.
Assistant: Claimed and recorded.
User: What it tells me is that I'm actually capable of patience when I decide to be, which I'd half stopped believing about myself. That's the takeaway. Nothing cosmic. Just that.
Assistant: Not cosmic, but real. Do you want this kept?
User: Yes. Keep it next to the wonky shelf one. Next time I'm about to skip a step, pull this out and show me the level shelf. That's what it's for.
Assistant: Filed beside the first shelf. Two shelves, one pair of entries.
User: Books are going on it tonight. The plants can retire.
Assistant: A well-earned retirement for the plants. Enjoy the books.

Session 14. Client on time. Mood described as "fine, a bit fed up". Client did not wish to return to the separation this week and instead spent the first part of the session on a minor recreational disappointment, which clinician accepted as a reasonable use of the time.

Client had attended a heated yoga class, booked as a trial, on the recommendation of a colleague. Client reported disliking it from the first ten minutes: "I went dizzy about twenty minutes in and had to kneel down, and I was queasy for the rest of the hour, and sweat was running into my eyes so I couldn't see the instructor anyway." Client left before the end.

Client attributed the poor experience squarely to their own decision: "That one's on me. I know perfectly well I hate being hot, and I booked it anyway because I didn't want to say no to her. Nobody made me go." Clinician noted the self-attribution without challenging it, as it appeared proportionate.

Client stated that the experience had, in a small way, closed a door: "That's it for evening classes for me. I've been trying them for a year and that was the last one. Tuesday nights are going to be something else from now on, I just don't know what yet." Clinician reflected the finality of this and client confirmed it, with some humour.

Client asked that the episode be noted in the record "so that when I next mention a class someone's recommended, you can remind me about the kneeling". Clinician agreed.

Remainder of session on scheduling and sleep diary. Risk: none. Plan: next session as scheduled.

They offered me the lead on the new programme today. Not the deputy, not "supporting". The lead. The director took me into the small meeting room, the one with the broken blind, and said it in about four sentences, and then asked if I wanted to think about it, and I said no, I don't need to think about it, yes.

I said yes. Out loud, first time, no hedging.

I know what I'd normally do with news like this. I'd fold it up small and put it away and tell people "oh, it's just a title" for a month until the shine wore off. I've always been like that with good feeling, I keep it on a short lead so it can't get away from me and so nobody can take it. I'm trying not to do that tonight. I'm trying to let it be as big as it is.

Rang my sister. She said "about time". The nephew asked if I was the boss of everybody and I said nearly.

No wine. Didn't even cross my mind until I wrote that sentence, which is its own kind of news.

She came to dinner. The friend from the pharmacy queue, from the old flat, from the funeral I didn't go to. I cooked the only thing I can cook for guests and she brought a bottle of the posh elderflower stuff without me having to say anything, which told me she'd been listening in the café.

It was easy. That's the astonishing thing. I'd braced for three hours of careful, and instead we were twenty minutes in and laughing about the landlord from the old place and the time the bath came through the ceiling. She had photos on her phone from that year, ones I'd never seen, and in one of them I'm asleep on the kitchen floor with a colander on my head and she's pointing at me and howling.

We talked about her dad. Properly. I asked about the funeral and she told me, and I listened, and at one point she stopped and said "you're allowed to ask, you know", and I said thank you.

She left at eleven. Hugged me in the doorway, and the hug was the old kind, the kind where you lean.

What it means, I think, is that some things can be mended even after a very long time, and that the mending doesn't have to be dramatic to be real. It can be a casserole and a colander photo. That's enough. That counts.

I washed up slowly. I didn't want the evening to be over yet, so I made it last another twenty minutes with the taps running and the radio low.

Sunday lunch at my sister's. Roast, slightly overdone, as always, and nobody minded, as always.

The nephew made me read the dinosaur book four times. I'm the one in this family who does the voices; my sister refuses on principle and her husband does them all in the same voice, which the nephew finds unacceptable. So it's me. The stegosaurus has a cold. The big one with the teeth is from the north. I've been doing these voices for three years and I will apparently be doing them until he's twelve.

After lunch I lay on their sofa with the sun coming through the big window straight onto my legs and had that heavy, warm, full-stomached feeling where your eyelids weigh about a kilo each. I dozed for twenty minutes with the nephew's feet in my ribs. Woke up to the smell of coffee and someone laughing in the kitchen.

We did the crossword, badly. My sister got the long one. I got the one about rivers, which she pointed out was "my corner". It is.

Drove home with the windows down and the radio on something I didn't recognise and didn't mind.

Nothing happened today. It was nice. That's all.

Lido this evening. Shouldn't have bothered.

The water was the coldest it's been all year and the lane was full of people doing butterfly badly, and I got kicked twice, and by the second length my fingers had gone white and I couldn't feel my feet at all, just a sort of distant thudding where they should be. Got out after six lengths. Sat in the changing room with my teeth going and my skin stinging all over as the blood came back and thought, why do I do this.

I'm the one who organises these. For four years I've been the lido person in our little group, the one who sends the "anyone fancy a swim" message and books the slot and brings the spare towel. Everyone else drifted off ages ago. It's just been me and the message for most of this year, and tonight it was just me and the message and a stranger's heel in my shoulder.

Well. That was the last one. I mean it this time. The lido era is over; something else will go in that slot on Thursdays and it is not going to involve a changing room. Decided, on the bench, with the teeth going. I'm not going to miss it, or I'll miss the idea of it and not the thing itself.

Bad evening. Tea, hot bath, bed.

In the family story I had been the sibling who left gatherings early for the wrong reasons. This year I became the one who drives everyone home, and I noticed that nobody remarked on it, which I take as the highest compliment available.

What the year taught me is that wanting a drink and needing one were never the same thing, and that I had spent a decade letting the first impersonate the second.

I keep this page so that on some future bad night I can open it and see, in my own words, that I have already done the difficult version of this and liked who I was on the other side.

The library book is one of those stories I tell at dinners when the conversation turns to small crimes. I borrowed a field guide to seashells from the branch library when I was about eleven and simply never took it back. It sat on my shelf through two house moves and a university degree. Every so often I would see the spine and my face would go hot, and I would put something in front of it. Then, in my late twenties, I walked into a different branch of the same system with the book in a tote bag, braced for a fine the size of a car payment, and the person at the counter scanned it, said "oh, this one's been written off," and dropped it on a trolley for resale. That was it. Fifteen years of minor dread, resolved in ten seconds by someone who did not look up.

I am clear about where that one sits: it was nobody's doing but mine. The library did not lose the book; I kept it.

What the whole thing taught me is that the penalty you imagine is almost always larger than the penalty that exists, and that the imagining is the actual cost. I tell this story at dinners partly because it is funny and partly so that whoever is at the table carrying their own overdue thing hears that the counter is kinder than the shelf. Mixed feelings, still. I am faintly ashamed of eleven-year-old me, and faintly proud of the tote bag.

The first half was lovely. Cool morning, my watch chirping the splits exactly where they should be, strangers on the bridge shouting my race number. Then somewhere past the twenty mile marker my legs turned to concrete, a dull heavy ache that went from the hips down and did not lift again. The last six miles were a walk-shuffle-walk beside a woman in a frog hat who was having the same day I was. We did not exchange names. We finished eleven seconds apart and hugged like family.

I know exactly whose doing the second half was. I went out too fast. Nobody made me; the pacer was right there and I ran away from her because the first ten felt free. That is on me and I am not going to dress it up as the weather or the course.

I don't, as a rule, let anyone see me struggle. I go quiet and get through it and tell people after. So walking down the middle of a main road with my face doing whatever it was doing, in front of several thousand people, was its own kind of finish line.

What it taught me is that the distance does not care about the plan, and that finishing badly is still finishing. I am prouder of the walking than of the running, which I did not expect to write.

I am keeping this entry so that the next time I stand on a start line with a number on my chest, I read it the night before and start slower. Mixed day. Medal is on the doorknob. Legs are on the sofa. I will decide what I think about all of it tomorrow.

text: Up, and by coach to Sir Ph. Warwicke’s, the streete being full of footballs, it being a great frost, and found him and Mr. Coventry walking in St. James’s Parke. I did my errand to him about the felling of the King’s timber in the forests, and then to my Lord of Oxford, Justice in Eyre, for his consent thereto, for want whereof my Lord Privy Seale stops the whole business. I found him in his lodgings, in but an ordinary furnished house and roome where he was, but I find him to be a man of good discreet replys. Thence to the Coffee-house, where certain newes that the Dutch have taken some of our colliers to the North; some say four, some say seven. Thence to the ‘Change a while, and so home to dinner and to the office, where we sat late, and then I to write my letters, and then to Sir W. Batten’s, who is going out of towne to Harwich to-morrow to set up a light-house there, which he hath lately got a patent from the King to set up, that will turne much to his profit. Here very merry, and so to my office again, where very late, and then home to supper and to bed, but sat up with my wife at cards till past two in the morning.

Up, and very angry with my boy for lying long a bed and forgetting his lute. To my office all the morning. At noon to the ‘Change, and so home to dinner. After dinner to Gresham College to my Lord Brunker and Commissioner Pett, taking, Mr. Castle with me there to discourse over his draught of a ship he is to build for us. Where I first found reason to apprehend Commissioner Pett to be a man of an ability extraordinary in any thing, for I found he did turn and wind Castle like a chicken in his business, and that most pertinently and mister-like, and great pleasure it was to me to hear them discourse, I, of late having studied something thereof, and my Lord Brunker is a very able person also himself in this sort of business, as owning himself to be a master in the business of all lines and Conicall Sections: Thence home, where very late at my office doing business to my content, though [God] knows with what ado it was that when I was out I could get myself to come home to my business, or when I was there though late would stay there from going abroad again. To supper and to bed. This evening, by a letter from Plymouth, I hear that two of our ships, the Leopard and another, in the Straights, are lost by running aground; and that three more had like to have been so, but got off, whereof Captain Allen one: and that a Dutch fleete are gone thither; which if they should meet with our lame ships, God knows what would become of them. This I reckon most sad newes; God make us sensible of it! This night, when I come home, I was much troubled to hear my poor canary bird, that I have kept these three or four years, is dead.

Up, and to White Hall about getting a privy seal for felling of the King’s timber for the navy, and to the Lords’ House to speak with my Lord Privy Seale about it, and so to the ‘Change, where to my last night’s ill news I met more. Spoke with a Frenchman who was taken, but released, by a Dutch man-of-war of thirty-six guns (with seven more of the like or greater ships), off the North Foreland, by Margett. Which is a strange attempt, that they should come to our teeth; but the wind being easterly, the wind that should bring our force from Portsmouth, will carry them away home. God preserve us against them, and pardon our making them in our discourse so contemptible an enemy! So home and to dinner, where Mr. Hollyard with us dined. So to the office, and there late till 11 at night and more, and then home to supper and to bed.

Up and walked to Mr. Povy’s by appointment, where I found him and Creed busy about fitting things for the Committee, and thence we to my Lord Ashly’s, where to see how simply, beyond all patience, Povy did again, by his many words and no understanding, confound himself and his business, to his disgrace, and rendering every body doubtfull of his being either a foole or knave, is very wonderfull. We broke up all dissatisfied, and referred the business to a meeting of Mr. Sherwin and others to settle, but here it was mighty strange methought to find myself sit herein Committee with my hat on, while Mr. Sherwin stood bare as a clerke, with his hat off to his Lord Ashlyand the rest, but I thank God I think myself never a whit the better man for all that. Thence with Creed to the ‘Change and Coffee-house, and so home, where a brave dinner, by having a brace of pheasants and very merry about Povy’s folly. So anon to the office, and there sitting very late, and then after a little time at Sir W. Batten’s, where I am mighty great and could if I thought it fit continue so, I to the office again, and there very late, and so home to the sorting of some of my books, and so to bed, the weather becoming pretty warm, and I think and hope the frost will break.

Up and by and by to my bookseller’s, and there did give thorough direction for the new binding of a great many of my old books, to make my whole study of the same binding, within very few. Thence to my Lady Sandwich’s, who sent for me this morning. Dined with her, and it was to get a letter of hers conveyed by a safe hand to my Lord’s owne hand at Portsmouth, which I did undertake. Here my Lady did begin to talk of what she had heard concerning Creed, of his being suspected to be a fanatique and a false fellow. I told her I thought he was as shrewd and cunning a man as any in England, and one that I would feare first should outwit me in any thing. To which she readily concurred. Thence to Mr. Povy’s by agreement, and there with Mr. Sherwin, Auditor Beale, and Creed and I hard at it very late about Mr. Povy’s accounts, but such accounts I never did see, or hope again to see in my days. At night, late, they gone, I did get him to put out of this account our sums that are in posse only yet, which he approved of when told, but would never have stayed it if I had been gone. Thence at 9 at night home, and so to supper vexed and my head akeing and to bed.

Up, and it being yesterday and to-day a great thaw it is not for a man to walk the streets, but took coach and to Mr. Povy’s, and there meeting all of us again agreed upon an answer to the Lords by and by, and thence we did come to Exeter House, and there was a witness of most furiously angry with him, because the other, as a foole, would needs say that the L26,000 was my Lord Peterborough’s account, and that he had nothing to do with it. The Lords did find fault also with our answer, but I think really my Lord Ashly would fain have the outside of an Exchequer,--[This word is blotted, and the whole sentence is confused.]--but when we come better to be examined. So home by coach, with my Lord Barkeley, who, by his discourse, I find do look upon Mr. Coventry as an enemy but yet professes great justice and pains. I at home after dinner to the office, and there sat all the afternoon and evening, and then home to supper and to bed. Memorandum. This day and yesterday, I think it is the change of the weather, I have a great deal of pain, but nothing like what I use to have. I can hardly keep myself loose, but on the contrary am forced to drive away my pain. Here I am so sleepy I cannot hold open my eyes, and therefore must be forced to break off this day’s passages more shortly than I would and should have done. This day was buried (but I could not be there) my cozen Percivall Angier; and yesterday I received the newes that Dr. Tom Pepys is dead, at Impington, for which I am but little sorry, not only because he would have been troublesome to us, but a shame to his family and profession; he was such a coxcomb.

Up and by coach to Westminster Hall and the Parliament House, and there spoke with Mr. Coventry and others about business and so back to the ‘Change, where no news more than that the Dutch have, by consent of all the Provinces, voted no trade to be suffered for eighteen months, but that they apply themselves wholly to the warr. a period as eighteen months, by a government so essentially commercial as that of the United Provinces, seems extraordinary. The fact was, that when in the beginning of the year 1665 the States General saw that the war with England was become inevitable, they took several vigorous measures, and determined to equip a formidable fleet, and with a view to obtain a sufficient number of men to man it, prohibited all navigation, especially in the great and small fisheries as they were then called, and in the whale fishery.  This measure appears to have resembled the embargoes so commonly resorted to in this country on similar occasions, rather than a total prohibition of trade.--B.] And they say it is very true, but very strange, for we use to believe they cannot support themselves without trade. Thence home to dinner and then to the office, where all the afternoon, and at night till very late, and then home to supper and bed, having a great cold, got on Sunday last, by sitting too long with my head bare, for Mercer to comb my hair and wash my eares.

Up, and busy all the morning, dined at home upon a hare pye, very good meat, and so to my office again, and in the afternoon by coach to attend the Council at White Hall, but come too late, so back with Mr. Gifford, a merchant, and he and I to the Coffee-house, where I met Mr. Hill, and there he tells me that he is to be Assistant to the Secretary of the Prize Office (Sir Ellis Layton), which is to be held at Sir Richard Ford’s, which, methinks, is but something low, but perhaps may bring him something considerable; but it makes me alter my opinion of his being so rich as to make a fortune for Mrs. Pickering. Thence home and visited Sir J. Minnes, who continues ill, but is something better; there he told me what a mad freaking fellow Sir Ellis Layton hath been, and is, and once at Antwerp was really mad. Thence to my office late, my cold troubling me, and having by squeezing myself in a coach hurt my testicles, but I hope will cease its pain without swelling. So home out of order, to supper and to bed.

Called up by Mr. Creed to discourse about some Tangier business, and he gone I made me ready and found Jane Welsh, Mr. Jervas his mayde, come to tell me that she was gone from her master, and is resolved to stick to this sweetheart of hers, one Harbing (a very sorry little fellow, and poor), which I did in a word or two endeavour to dissuade her from, but being unwilling to keep her long at my house, I sent her away and by and by followed her to the Exchange, and thence led her about down to the 3 Cranes, and there took boat for the Falcon, and at a house looking into the fields there took up and sat an hour or two talking and discoursing .... Thence having endeavoured to make her think of making herself happy by staying out her time with her master and other counsels, but she told me she could not do it, for it was her fortune to have this man, though she did believe it would be to her ruine, which is a strange, stupid thing, to a fellow of no kind of worth in the world and a beggar to boot. Thence away to boat again and landed her at the Three Cranes again, and I to the Bridge, and so home, and after shifting myself, being dirty, I to the ‘Change, and thence to Mr. Povy’s and there dined, and thence with him and Creed to my Lord Bellasses’, and there debated a great while how to put things in order against his going, and so with my Lord in his coach to White Hall, and with him to my Lord Duke of Albemarle, finding him at cards. After a few dull words or two, I away to White Hall again, and there delivered a letter to the Duke of Yorke about our Navy business, and thence walked up and down in the gallery, talking with Mr. Slingsby, who is a very ingenious person, about the Mint and coynage of money. Among other things, he argues that there being L700,000 coined in the Rump time, and by all the Treasurers of that time, it being their opinion that the Rump money was in all payments, one with another, about a tenth part of all their money. Then, says he, to my question, the nearest guess we can make is, that the money passing up and down in business is L7,000,000. To another question of mine he made me fully understand that the old law of prohibiting bullion to be exported, is, and ever was a folly and an injury, rather than good. Arguing thus, that if the exportations exceed importations, then the balance must be brought home in money, which, when our merchants know cannot be carried out again, they will forbear to bring home in money, but let it lie abroad for trade, or keepe in foreign banks: or if our importations exceed our exportations, then, to keepe credit, the merchants will and must find ways of carrying out money by stealth, which is a most easy thing to do, and is every where done; and therefore the law against it signifies nothing in the world. Besides, that it is seen, that where money is free, there is great plenty; where it is restrained, as here, there is a great want, as in Spayne. These and many other fine discourses I had from him. Thence by coach home (to see Sir J. Minnes first), who is still sick, and I doubt worse than he seems to be. Mrs. Turner here took me into her closet, and there did give me a glass of most pure water, and shewed me her Rocke, which indeed is a very noble thing but a very bawble. So away to my office, where late, busy, and then home to supper and to bed.

Up and with Sir W. Batten to Westminster, where to speak at the House with my Lord Bellasses, and am cruelly vexed to see myself put upon businesses so uncertainly about getting ships for Tangier being ordered, a servile thing, almost every day. So to the ‘Change, back by coach with Sir W. Batten, and thence to the Crowne, a taverne hard by, with Sir W. Rider and Cutler, where we alone, a very good dinner. Thence home to the office, and there all the afternoon late. The office being up, my wife sent for me, and what was it but to tell me how Jane carries herself, and I must put her away presently. But I did hear both sides and find my wife much in fault, and the grounds of all the difference is my wife’s fondness of Tom, to the being displeased with all the house beside to defend the boy, which vexes me, but I will cure it. Many high words between my wife and I, but the wench shall go, but I will take a course with the boy, for I fear I have spoiled him already. Thence to the office, to my accounts, and there at once to ease my mind I have made myself debtor to Mr. Povy for the L117 5s. got with so much joy the last month, but seeing that it is not like to be kept without some trouble and question, I do even discharge my mind of it, and so if I come now to refund it, as I fear I shall, I shall now be ne’er a whit the poorer for it, though yet it is some trouble to me to be poorer by such a sum than I thought myself a month since. But, however, a quiet mind and to be sure of my owne is worth all. The Lord be praised for what I have, which is this month come down to L1257. I staid up about my accounts till almost two in the morning.

Up, and all the morning full of business at the office. At noon dined with Mr. Povy, and then to the getting some business looked over of his, and then I to my Lord Chancellor’s, where to have spoke with the Duke of Albemarle, but the King and Council busy, I could not; then to the Old Exchange and there of my new pretty seamstress bought four bands, and so home, where I found my house mighty neat and clean. Then to my office late, till past 12, and so home to bed. The French Embassadors natural son of Henry IV. and brother of Henrietta Maria, and M. de Courtin.--B.] are come incognito before their train, which will hereafter be very pompous. It is thought they come to get our King to joyne with the King of France in helping him against Flanders, and they to do the like to us against Holland. We have laine a good while with a good fleete at Harwich. The Dutch not said yet to be out. We, as high as we make our shew, I am sure, are unable to set out another small fleete, if this should be worsted. Wherefore, God send us peace! I cry. 9th (Lord’s day). To church with my wife in the morning, in her new light-coloured silk gowne, which is, with her new point, very noble. Dined at home, and in the afternoon to Fanchurch, the little church in the middle of Fanchurch Streete, where a very few people and few of any rank. Thence, after sermon, home, and in the evening walking in the garden, my Lady Pen and her daughter walked with my wife and I, and so to my house to eat with us, and very merry, and so broke up and to bed.

Up, and to the Duke of Albemarle’s, and thence to White Hall to a Committee for Tangier, where new disorder about Mr. Povy’s accounts, that I think I shall never be settled in my business of Treasurer for him. Here Captain Cooke met me, and did seem discontented about my boy Tom’s having no time to mind his singing nor lute, which I answered him fully in, that he desired me that I would baste his coate. So home and to the ‘Change, and thence to the “Old James” to dine with Sir W. Rider, Cutler, and Mr. Deering, upon the business of hemp, and so hence to White Hall to have attended the King and Lord Chancellor about the debts of the navy and to get some money, but the meeting failed. So my Lord Brunkard took me and Sir Thomas Harvy in his coach to the Parke, which is very troublesome with the dust; and ne’er a great beauty there to-day but Mrs. Middleton, and so home to my office, where Mr. Warren proposed my getting of L100 to get him a protection for a ship to go out, which I think I shall do. So home to supper and to bed.

Up, and to White Hall to a Committee of Tangier, where, contrary to all expectation, my Lord Ashly, being vexed with Povy’s accounts, did propose it as necessary that Povy should be still continued Treasurer of Tangier till he had made up his accounts; and with such arguments as, I confess, I was not prepared to answer, but by putting off of the discourse, and so, I think, brought it right again; but it troubled me so all the day after, and night too, that I was not quiet, though I think it doubtfull whether I shall be much the worse for it or no, if it should come to be so. Dined at home and thence to White Hall again (where I lose most of my time now-a-days to my great trouble, charge, and loss of time and benefit), and there, after the Council rose, Sir G. Carteret, my Lord Brunkard, Sir Thomas Harvy, and myself, down to my Lord Treasurer’s chamber to him and the Chancellor, and the Duke of Albemarle; and there I did give them a large account of the charge of the Navy, and want of money. But strange to see how they held up their hands crying, “What shall we do?” Says my Lord Treasurer, “Why, what means all this, Mr. Pepys? This is true, you say; but what would you have me to do? I have given all I can for my life. Why will not people lend their money? Why will they not trust the King as well as Oliver? Why do our prizes come to nothing, that yielded so much heretofore?” And this was all we could get, and went away without other answer, which is one of the saddest things that, at such a time as this, with the greatest action on foot that ever was in England, nothing should be minded, but let things go on of themselves do as well as they can. So home, vexed, and going to my Lady Batten’s, there found a great many women with her, in her chamber merry, my Lady Pen and her daughter, among others; where my Lady Pen flung me down upon the bed, and herself and others, one after another, upon me, and very merry we were, and thence I home and called my wife with my Lady Pen to supper, and very merry as I could be, being vexed as I was. So home to bed.

Up, and betimes to Mr. Povy, being desirous to have an end of my trouble of mind touching my Tangier business, whether he hath any desire of accepting what my Lord Ashly offered, of his becoming Treasurer again; and there I did, with a seeming most generous spirit, offer him to take it back again upon his owne terms; but he did answer to me that he would not above all things in the world, at which I was for the present satisfied; but, going away thence and speaking with Creed, he puts me in doubt that the very nature of the thing will require that he be put in again; and did give me the reasons of the auditors, which, I confess, are so plain, that I know not how to withstand them. But he did give me most ingenious advice what to do in it, and anon, my Lord Barkeley and some of the Commissioners coming together, though not in a meeting, I did procure that they should order Povy’s payment of his remain of accounts to me; which order if it do pass will put a good stop to the fastening of the thing upon me. At noon Creed and I to a cook’s shop at Charing Cross, and there dined and had much discourse, and his very good upon my business, and upon other things, among the rest upon Will Howe’s dissembling with us, we discovering one to another his carriage to us, present and absent, being a very false fellow. Thence to White Hall again, and there spent the afternoon, and then home to fetch a letter for the Council, and so back to White Hall, where walked an hour with Mr. Wren, of my Lord Chancellor’s, and Mr. Ager, and then to Unthanke’s and called my wife, and with her through the city to Mile-End Greene, and eat some creame and cakes and so back home, and I a little at the office, and so home to supper and to bed. This morning I was saluted with newes that the fleetes, ours and the Dutch, were engaged, and that the guns were heard at Walthamstow to play all yesterday, and that Captain Teddiman’s legs were shot off in the Royall Katherine. But before night I hear the contrary, both by letters of my owne and messengers thence, that they were all well of our side and no enemy appears yet, and that the Royall Katherine is come to the fleete, and likely to prove as good a ship as any the King hath, of which I am heartily glad, both for Christopher Pett’s sake and Captain Teddiman that is in her.

Up and to the Duke of Albemarle’s, where he shewed me Mr. Coventry’s letters, how three Dutch privateers are taken, in one whereof Everson’s’ son is captaine. But they have killed poor Captaine Golding in The Diamond. Two of them, one of 32 and the other of 20 odd guns, did stand stoutly up against her, which hath 46, and the Yarmouth that hath 52 guns, and as many more men as they. So that they did more than we could expect, not yielding till many of their men were killed. And Everson, when he was brought before the Duke of Yorke, and was observed to be shot through the hat, answered, that he wished it had gone through his head, rather than been taken. One thing more is written: that two of our ships the other day appearing upon the coast of Holland, they presently fired their beacons round the country to give notice. And newes is brought the King, that the Dutch Smyrna fleete is seen upon the back of Scotland; and thereupon the King hath wrote to the Duke, that he do appoint a fleete to go to the Northward to try to meet them coming home round: which God send! Thence to White Hall; where the King seeing me, did come to me, and calling me by name, did discourse with me about the ships in the River: and this is the first time that ever I knew the King did know me personally; so that hereafter I must not go thither, but with expectation to be questioned, and to be ready to give good answers. So home, and thence with Creed, who come to dine with me, to the Old James, where we dined with Sir W. Rider and Cutler, and, by and by, being called by my wife, we all to a play, “The Ghosts,” at the Duke’s house, but a very simple play. Thence up and down, with my wife with me, to look [for] Sir Ph. Warwicke (Mr. Creed going from me), but missed of him and so home, and late and busy at my office. So home to supper and to bed. This day was left at my house a very neat silver watch, by one Briggs, a scrivener and sollicitor, at which I was angry with my wife for receiving, or, at least, for opening the box wherein it was, and so far witnessing our receipt of it, as to give the messenger 5s. for bringing it; but it can’t be helped, and I will endeavour to do the man a kindnesse, he being a friend of my uncle Wight’s.

Up and to Sir Philip Warwicke, and walked with him an houre with great delight in the Parke about Sir G. Carteret’s accounts, and the endeavours that he hath made to bring Sir G. Carteret to show his accounts and let the world see what he receives and what he pays. Thence home to the office, where I find Sir J. Minnes come home from Chatham, and Sir W. Batten both this morning from Harwich, where they have been these 7 or 8 days. At noon with my wife and Mr. Moore by water to Chelsey about my Privy Seale for Tangier, but my Lord Privy Seale was gone abroad, and so we, without going out of the boat, forced to return, and found him not at White Hall. So I to Sir Philip Warwicke and with him to my Lord Treasurer, who signed my commission for Tangier-Treasurer and the docquet of my Privy Seale, for the monies to be paid to me. Thence to White Hall to Mr. Moore again, and not finding my Lord I home, taking my wife and woman up at Unthanke’s. Late at my office, then to supper and to bed.

Up by five o’clock, and by water to White Hall; and there took coach, and with Mr. Moore to Chelsy; where, after all my fears what doubts and difficulties my Lord Privy Seale would make at my Tangier Privy Seale, he did pass it at first reading, without my speaking with him. And then called me in, and was very civil to me. I passed my time in contemplating (before I was called in) the picture of my Lord’s son’s lady, a most beautiful woman, and most like to Mrs. Butler. Thence very much joyed to London back again, and found out Mr. Povy; told him this; and then went and left my Privy Seale at my Lord Treasurer’s; and so to the ‘Change, and thence to Trinity-House; where a great dinner of Captain Crisp, who is made an Elder Brother. And so, being very pleasant at dinner, away home, Creed with me; and there met Povy; and we to Gresham College, where we saw some experiments upon a hen, a dogg, and a cat, of the Florence poyson. of Florentine poison sent for by his Majesty from Florence, on purpose to have those experiments related of the efficacy thereof, tried by the Society.”  The poison had little effect upon the kitten (Birch’s “History;” vol. ii., p. 31).] The first it made for a time drunk, but it come to itself again quickly; the second it made vomitt mightily, but no other hurt. The third I did not stay to see the effect of it, being taken out by Povy. He and I walked below together, he giving me most exceeding discouragements in the getting of money (whether by design or no I know not, for I am now come to think him a most cunning fellow in most things he do, but his accounts), and made it plain to me that money will be hard to get, and that it is to be feared Backewell hath a design in it to get the thing forced upon himself. This put me into a cruel melancholy to think I may lose what I have had so near my hand; but yet something may be hoped for which to-morrow will shew. He gone, Creed and I together a great while consulting what to do in this case, and after all I left him to do what he thought fit in his discourse to-morrow with my Lord Ashly. So home, and in my way met with Mr. Warren, from whom my hopes I fear will fail of what I hoped for, by my getting him a protection. But all these troubles will if not be over, yet we shall see the worst of there in a day or two. So to my office, and thence to supper, and my head akeing, betimes, that is by 10 or 11 o’clock, to bed.

Up, and all the morning busy at the office. At noon dined, and Mr. Povy by agreement with me (where his boldness with Mercer, poor innocent wench, did make both her and me blush, to think how he were able to debauch a poor girl if he had opportunity) at a dish or two of plain meat of his own choice. After dinner comes Creed and then Andrews, where want of money to Andrews the main discourse, and at last in confidence of Creed’s judgement I am resolved to spare him 4 or L500 of what lies by me upon the security of some Tallys. This went against my heart to begin, but when obtaining Mr. Creed to joyne with me we do resolve to assist Mr. Andrews. Then anon we parted, and I to my office, where late, and then home to supper and to bed. This night I am told the first play is played in White Hall noon-hall, which is now turned to a house of playing. I had a great mind, but could not go to see it.

Up, and Mr. Caesar, my boy’s lute-master, being come betimes to teach him, I did speak with him seriously about the boy, what my mind was, if he did not look after his lute and singing that I would turn him away; which I hope will do some good upon the boy. All the morning busy at the office. At noon dined at home, and then to the office again very busy till very late, and so home to supper and to bed. My wife making great preparation to go to Court to Chappell to-morrow. This day I have newes from Mr. Coventry that the fleete is sailed yesterday from Harwich to the coast of Holland to see what the Dutch will do. God go along with them! 23rd (Lord’s day). Mr. Povy, according to promise, sent his coach betimes, and I carried my wife and her woman to White Hall Chappell and set them in the Organ Loft, and I having left to untruss went to the Harp and Ball and there drank also, and entertained myself in talke with the mayde of the house, a pretty mayde and very modest. Thence to the Chappell and heard the famous young Stillingfleete, whom I knew at Cambridge, and is now newly admitted one of the King’s chaplains; and was presented, they say, to my Lord Treasurer for St. Andrew’s, Holborne, where he is now minister, with these words: that they (the Bishops of Canterbury, London, and another) believed he is the ablest young man to preach the Gospel of any since the Apostles. He did make the most plain, honest, good, grave sermon, in the most unconcerned and easy yet substantial manner, that ever I heard in my life, upon the words of Samuell to the people, “Fear the Lord in truth with all your heart, and remember the great things that he hath done for you.” It being proper to this day, the day of the King’s Coronation. Thence to Mr. Povy’s, where mightily treated, and Creed with us. But Lord! to see how Povy overdoes every thing in commending it, do make it nauseous to me, and was not (by reason of my large praise of his house) over acceptable to my wife. Thence after dinner Creed and we by coach took the ayre in the fields beyond St. Pancras, it raining now and then, which it seems is most welcome weather, and then all to my house, where comes Mr. Hill, Andrews, and Captain Taylor, and good musique, but at supper to hear the arguments we had against Taylor concerning a Corant, he saying that the law of a dancing Corant is to have every barr to end in a pricked crochet and quaver, which I did deny, was very strange. It proceeded till I vexed him, but all parted friends, for Creed and I to laugh at when he was gone. After supper, Creed and I together to bed, in Mercer’s bed, and so to sleep.

All the morning busy at the office. In the afternoon to my Lord Treasurer’s, and there got my Lord Treasurer to sign the warrant for my striking of tallys, and so doing many jobbs in my way home, and there late writeing letters, being troubled in my mind to hear that Sir W. Batten and Sir J. Minnes do take notice that I am now-a-days much from the office upon no office business, which vexes me, and will make me mind my business the better, I hope in God; but what troubles me more is, that I do omit to write, as I should do, to Mr. Coventry, which I must not do, though this night I minded it so little as to sleep in the middle of my letter to him, and committed forty blotts and blurrs in my letter to him, but of this I hope never more to be guilty, if I have not already given him sufficient offence. So, late home, and to bed. 30th (Lord’s day). Up and to my office alone all the morning, making up my monthly accounts, which though it hath been very intricate, and very great disbursements and receipts and odd reckonings, yet I differed not from the truth; viz.: between my first computing what my profit ought to be and then what my cash and debts do really make me worth, not above 10s., which is very much, and I do much value myself upon the account, and herein I with great joy find myself to have gained this month above L100 clear, and in the whole to be worth above L1400, the greatest sum I ever yet was worth. Thence home to dinner, and there find poor Mr. Spong walking at my door, where he had knocked, and being told I was at the office staid modestly there walking because of disturbing me, which methinks was one of the most modest acts (of a man that hath no need of being so to me) that ever I knew in my life. He dined with me, and then after dinner to my closet, where abundance of mighty pretty discourse, wherein, in a word, I find him the man of the world that hath of his own ingenuity obtained the most in most things, being withall no scholler. He gone, I took boat and down to Woolwich and Deptford, and made it late home, and so to supper and to bed. Thus I end this month in great content as to my estate and gettings: in much trouble as to the pains I have taken, and the rubs I expect yet to meet with, about the business of Tangier. The fleete, with about 106 ships upon the coast of Holland, in sight of the Dutch, within the Texel. Great fears of the sickenesse here in the City, it being said that two or three houses are already shut up. God preserve as all!

Up and to the office, where sat all the morning, at noon to the ‘Change, and there did some business, and home to dinner, whither Creed comes, and after dinner I put on my new silke camelott sute; the best that ever I wore in my life, the sute costing me above L24. In this I went with Creed to Goldsmiths’ Hall, to the burial of Sir Thomas Viner; which Hall, and Haberdashers also, was so full of people, that we were fain for ease and coolness to go forth to Pater Noster Row, to choose a silke to make me a plain ordinary suit. That done, we walked to Cornehill, and there at Mr. Cade’s’ stood in the balcon and saw all the funeral, which was with the blue-coat boys and old men, all the Aldermen, and Lord Mayor, &c., and the number of the company very great; the greatest I ever did see for a taverne. Hither come up to us Dr. Allen, and then Mr. Povy and Mr. Fox. The show being over, and my discourse with Mr. Povy, I took coach and to Westminster Hall, where I took the fairest flower, and by coach to Tothill Fields for the ayre till it was dark. I ‘light, and in with the fairest flower to eat a cake, and there did do as much as was safe with my flower, and that was enough on my part. Broke up, and away without any notice, and, after delivering the rose where it should be, I to the Temple and ‘light, and come to the middle door, and there took another coach, and so home to write letters, but very few, God knows, being by my pleasure made to forget everything that is. The coachman that carried [us] cannot know me again, nor the people at the house where we were. Home to bed, certain news being come that our fleete is in sight of the Dutch ships.

Up and to White Hall, where Sir G. Carteret did go with me to Secretary Morris, and prevailed with him to let Mr. Hater be released upon bail for his appearance. So I at a loss how to get another besides myself, and got Mr. Hunt, who did patiently stay with me all the morning at Secretary Morris’s chamber, Mr. Hater being sent for with his keeper, and at noon comes in the Secretary, and upon entering [into] recognizances, he for L200, and Mr. Hunt and I for L100 each for his appearance upon demand, he was released, it costing him, I think, above L3. I thence home, vexed to be kept from the office all the morning, which I had not been in many months before, if not some years. At home to dinner, and all the afternoon at the office, where late at night, and much business done, then home to supper and to bed. All this day by all people upon the River, and almost every where else hereabout were heard the guns, our two fleets for certain being engaged; which was confirmed by letters from Harwich, but nothing particular: and all our hearts full of concernment for the Duke, and I particularly for my Lord Sandwich and Mr. Coventry after his Royall Highnesse. 4th (Sunday). Up and at my chamber all the forenoon, at evening my accounts, which I could not do sooner, for the last month, and, blessed be God! am worth L1400 odd money, something more than ever I was yet in the world. Dined very well at noon, and then to my office, and there and in the garden discoursed with several people about business, among others Mr. Howell, the turner, who did give me so good a discourse about the practices of the Paymaster J. Fenn that I thought fit to recollect all when he was gone, and have entered it down to be for ever remembered. Thence to my chamber again to settle my Tangier accounts against tomorrow and some other things, and with great joy ended them, and so to supper, where a good fowl and tansy, and so to bed. Newes being come that our fleete is pursuing the Dutch, who, either by cunning, or by being worsted, do give ground, but nothing more for certain. Late to bed upon my papers being quite finished.

Waked in the morning before 4 o’clock with great pain to piss, and great pain in pissing by having, I think, drank too great a draught of cold drink before going to bed. But by and by to sleep again, and then rose and to the office, where very busy all the morning, and at noon to dinner with Sir G. Carteret to his house with all our Board, where a good pasty and brave discourse. But our great fear was some fresh news of the fleete, but not from the fleete, all being said to be well and beaten the Dutch, but I do not give much belief to it, and indeed the news come from Sir W. Batten at Harwich, and writ so simply that we all made good mirth of it. Thence to the office, where upon Sir G. Carteret’s accounts, to my great vexation there being nothing done by the Controller to right the King therein. I thence to my office and wrote letters all the afternoon, and in the evening by coach to Sir Ph. Warwicke’s about my Tangier business to get money, and so to my Lady Sandwich’s, who, poor lady, expects every hour to hear of my Lord; but in the best temper, neither confident nor troubled with fear, that I ever did see in my life. She tells me my Lord Rochester is now declaredly out of hopes of Mrs. Mallett, and now she is to receive notice in a day or two how the King stands inclined to the giving leave for my Lord Hinchingbroke to look after her, and that being done to bring it to an end shortly. Thence by coach home, and to my office a little, and so before 12 o’clock home and to bed.
